title: Spinning Lincolnshire Longwool
subtitle: Working with a coarse, lustrous longwool breed on wheel or spindle
excerpt: Lincolnshire Longwool is one of the longest-stapled British wool breeds, with individual locks running 15 to 30 cm and a noticeable lustre. Spun worsted-style, it produces a strong, hard-wearing yarn suited to rugs, floor cushions, and warp threads.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional British longwool spinning practice. Lincolnshire Longwool is documented in textile and agricultural records from the 18th century onward as one of England's premier commercial wool breeds; the spinning characteristics described here draw on standard guild workshop guidance for longwool breeds.

glossaryTerms.definition: A spinning technique where fibres are combed parallel before spinning and drafting happens ahead of the twist, producing a smooth, strong yarn.
The length of an individual lock or aligned group of wool fibres from a fleece, measured before washing or combing.
The natural sheen of a wool fibre, determined by the scale structure of the fibre surface. Longwool breeds have high lustre; fine breeds like Merino have little.

attrs.title: Wool dust
attrs.body: Longwool combing and prepping throws coarse fibre dust. Work in a ventilated space and damp-mop the floor afterwards.

items.name: Spinning wheel with a larger whorl ratio (e.g. 5:1 or 6:1)

content.text: Longwool locks are best prepared by combing or hackling to align the long fibres parallel before spinning. Draw each lock through the hackle teeth once or twice to straighten the fibres and remove short breaks. If you are spinning directly from the raw fleece, open each lock by hand, pulling from the cut end to the tip, before presenting it to the wheel. Avoid carding Lincolnshire Longwool: the drum-carding action shortens the long fibres and destroys the alignment that gives the yarn its strength and sheen.

Set the wheel to a lower ratio (5:1 to 7:1) and a fairly open tension. The long drafting zone required by a 20 to 30 cm lock means you need to hold the fibre supply further from the orifice than with short-staple breeds. Draft with the worsted draw: pinch the fibres behind the twist with the front hand, allow a short length of untwisted fibre to extend forward, then release the front hand and allow twist to run into the drafted zone. The long staple means the drafting zone extends 15 to 25 cm back from the pinch point.

Longwool needs less twist than fine wool for the same yarn weight. The fibres are long and grip each other strongly over their length; over-twisting produces a wiry, inelastic yarn that is stiff to weave or knit. Spin to a moderate twist and test regularly by drafting off a short length and releasing it: the yarn should hold its ply without kinking back sharply. Wind onto the bobbin with steady take-up tension to avoid coiling on the bobbin unevenly.

Ply two singles together in the opposite twist direction for a balanced 2-ply. Skein the yarn on the niddy-noddy and soak in warm water for five minutes. Snap the skein to set the twist, then hang to dry under slight tension to keep the lustre visible. Lincolnshire Longwool yarn blooms very little after washing: the finished skein looks much as it did on the bobbin. A single wet-finishing pass is sufficient.

items.problem: The singles break frequently at the wheel
items.cause: The twist ratio is too high or the tension too tight, over-twisting the singles and causing them to snap at weak points in the lock
items.fix: Reduce the drive-band tension and lower the whorl ratio. Long locks need less twist than short; if the singles feel wiry before you even ply them, the twist is already too high.

items.problem: The finished yarn has no lustre
items.cause: The fibre was carded rather than combed, or the locks were pulled from tip to cut rather than cut to tip during preparation, breaking the fibre alignment
items.fix: Prepare by hackling or combing only, always drawing from the cut end toward the tip to align the scales correctly.
